subtypes.name: Word problem: pick the system that models it
subtypes.tell: You get a story with two unknown quantities, each defined by a letter in the stem, and all four answer choices are pairs of equations. Nothing asks for a number. Usually one fact is a total count and the other is a total value, such as money, points or distance.
subtypes.method: 1) Write the count equation: the two unknowns add to the total number of items, hours or people. 2) Write the value equation: rate or price times each unknown, added together, equals the total value. 3) Pick the choice that matches both. Often you can rule out two choices using only the count equation.
subtypes.desmos: Mostly not useful, because the task is translating words, not calculating. If you are unsure, you can solve the story mentally with a plausible pair of values and graph each choice to see which one passes through it, but reading the rates directly is faster.
subtypes.trap: The wrong choices swap which rate goes with which variable, flip a 'times as many' relationship (writing Connor = k·Maria as Maria = k·Connor), put the per-item rate into the count equation, or use a percent discount where they should use the percent that remains (0.8, not 0.2).

subtypes.name: Word problem: solve for how many
subtypes.tell: The same count-and-value story as above, but the question asks for the number of one specific item, and the choices are single numbers.
subtypes.method: 1) Write the count equation and the value equation. 2) Multiply the count equation by the smaller rate and subtract it from the value equation. The other variable cancels, and you divide the leftover total by the difference in rates. 3) Check that you answered for the item the question named.
subtypes.desmos: Type both equations with x and y and tap the intersection. Or use x+y=T and ax+by=V directly. Keep track of which letter stands for which item.
subtypes.trap: You solve correctly and then report the other quantity (adults instead of children, magazines instead of novels). That value is always one of the wrong choices.

subtypes.name: Bare system with one variable already isolated
subtypes.tell: Two equations with no story, and one of them already reads y = … or x = … (or a single variable equals a number). The question asks for the solution pair or for one variable.
subtypes.method: 1) Substitute the isolated expression into the other equation. 2) Solve the resulting one-variable equation. 3) If the question asks for the other variable, substitute back. For choices given as pairs, you can instead plug each pair into the harder equation.
subtypes.desmos: Very effective. Enter both equations and click the intersection to read (x, y). Fractions and decimals work as typed. For fill-in answers, read the exact coordinate, and if it is a repeating decimal, convert it to a fraction.
subtypes.trap: You find the first variable and stop, when the question wanted the other one. The value of the variable they didn't ask for is almost always one of the choices. Sign errors when distributing a negative during substitution are the other common source of wrong answers.

subtypes.name: Add or subtract the equations to get what they ask for
subtypes.tell: Both equations are in standard form, and one variable has opposite or equal coefficients across them (+3y and −3y, for example). Or the question asks for an expression like x + y, 2x − y or x/y instead of a single variable.
subtypes.method: 1) Look at the coefficients before doing anything. 2) Add the equations if the coefficients are opposites, or subtract if they are equal. One variable disappears, or the target expression appears directly. 3) Divide if needed. Don't solve for both variables unless you have to.
subtypes.desmos: Graph both equations, tap the intersection, then type the target expression using those coordinates, or define x and y with sliders set to those values. This is reliable when the arithmetic gets messy.
subtypes.trap: The wrong choices are the value of x, the value of y, or the other variable's value, when the question asked for the one that elimination isolates or for a combined expression. You also lose time if you solve the whole system by substitution.

subtypes.name: Find the constant so the system has no solution or infinitely many
subtypes.tell: The stem says a letter 'is a constant' and states that the system has no solution or infinitely many solutions. The question asks for the constant's value, often as a fill-in answer.
subtypes.method: 1) Put both equations in the same form (standard Ax + By = C, or y = mx + b). 2) No solution: set the x/y coefficient ratios equal (same slope) and make sure the constants are NOT in that ratio. Infinitely many: every ratio, including the constants, must match. 3) Solve that ratio equation for the constant.
subtypes.desmos: Use a slider for the constant and adjust it until the lines are parallel (no solution) or on top of each other (infinitely many). This helps confirm your answer but is slow for finding exact or fractional values. Setting the slopes equal algebraically is faster.
subtypes.trap: You match the constant terms instead of the coefficients, or you forget to rearrange first, so the variables are on different sides and the ratio is wrong. For 'no solution' questions, a wrong choice is a value that makes the lines identical rather than parallel.

subtypes.name: Choose the equation or system with a given number of solutions
subtypes.tell: The question gives you one equation and asks which second equation 'could be' in the system given that it has no solution, infinitely many solutions or at least one solution. Or it asks which of four whole systems has no solution. Some versions use a Roman-numeral I/II format. A variation asks which point lies on both graphs 'for each real number', which signals that the lines coincide.
subtypes.method: 1) Rewrite everything so x, y and the constant are in the same positions. 2) Compare ratios. Scaling one equation to the other means infinitely many solutions (same line). The same x/y ratio with a different constant means no solution (parallel lines). A different x/y ratio means exactly one solution. 3) 'At least one solution' allows both 'one' and 'infinitely many'.
subtypes.desmos: Graph the given equation with each choice. Two lines on top of each other mean infinitely many solutions, parallel lines mean none, and crossing lines mean one. This is quick for multiple choice. For the coincident-point version, graph the equation and check which choice's point lies on the line.
subtypes.trap: You choose a parallel line when the question wanted the same line, or the reverse. On 'at least one solution' questions, you might wrongly reject the equivalent equation because it isn't exactly one solution.

subtypes.name: Read a system from its graph (or its graph from the system)
subtypes.tell: The stem includes a graph of two lines. The question asks either for the solution to the system (the choices are coordinate pairs) or which pair of equations or functions matches the lines shown, sometimes with real-world axis labels.
subtypes.method: Solution: 1) Find the intersection point and read its x first, then its y. Equations: 1) For each line, read the y-intercept and one other grid point, and compute the slope. 2) Match the slope and intercept to the choices, and rule out choices that fail on either one.
subtypes.desmos: For matching equations, type in the choices and see which pair overlays the picture. For reading a solution, the graph already gives it, so the calculator adds nothing unless you want to type the lines in and confirm the intersection.
subtypes.trap: The wrong choices are points that lie on only one line (such as an intercept), a point on neither line, or the intersection with x and y swapped. For matching equations, the slopes or intercepts are assigned to the wrong lines, or a slope has the wrong sign.

subtypes.name: Read center/radius from standard form
subtypes.tell: You see an equation already in the form (x − h)² + (y − k)² = number, sometimes with fractions or a non-perfect-square constant. The question asks for the center, the radius, the diameter, or which equation matches a given center and radius. The answer choices often differ only in signs or in r versus r².
subtypes.method: 1) The center is (h, k), so flip the sign of each number inside the parentheses. 2) The radius is the square root of the constant on the right. 3) If they ask for the diameter, double the radius. If you have to build the equation, square the radius before you write it on the right.
subtypes.desmos: Type the equation and Desmos draws the circle. Click the leftmost and rightmost points, and half the horizontal distance between them is the radius. This is a useful check, but reading the numbers straight off the equation is faster.
subtypes.trap: You give the constant as the radius without taking its square root, you keep the signs from inside the parentheses as the center coordinates, or you answer with the radius when the question asked for the diameter.

subtypes.name: Expanded circle equation / complete the square / scaled circle
subtypes.tell: The equation has loose x², y², x and y terms, like x² + y² + ax + by + c = 0, and nothing is grouped into squares. Or the question describes a second circle with the same center and a radius (or diameter) that is a multiple of the first, then asks for a constant in its expanded equation or for an unknown coordinate of a point on it.
subtypes.method: 1) Complete the square: add (a/2)² and (b/2)² to both sides to get standard form. 2) Read off the center and r². 3) For a scaled circle, multiply r by the factor, which means r² goes up by the factor squared. Then write the new equation, expand it if the question wants a constant, or plug in the given point.
subtypes.desmos: Type the expanded equation exactly as given and Desmos graphs the circle, so you can read the center and radius off the graph. To find a missing constant, add a slider for it and adjust until the circle has the required center or radius, or passes through the given point.
subtypes.trap: You forget to add the completing-the-square constants to the right side, or you double r² instead of multiplying it by 4 when the radius is doubled. Another trap is treating 'twice the diameter' as different from 'twice the radius', when both mean the radius doubles.

subtypes.name: Arc length and central angle as a fraction of the circle
subtypes.tell: The question mentions an arc, a central angle, the circumference, or a diameter or radius. You're given two of these (arc length, arc measure, radius or circumference) and asked for the third, or for what fraction of the circle an arc is. Sometimes there's a figure where the central angle comes from perpendicular diameters.
subtypes.method: 1) Set up arc/circumference = angle/360° (or angle/2π in radians). 2) Plug in what you know and solve for the missing piece. 3) Remember that an arc's degree measure equals its central angle, and that the diameter is 2r.
subtypes.trap: You use the arc's degree measure as its length, or mix up radius and diameter when you work out the circumference (2πr versus πd). Another trap is multiplying by the fraction when you should divide, or the reverse, when you go back from an arc to the whole circumference.

subtypes.name: Convert between radians and degrees
subtypes.tell: The question gives an angle in radians (usually a fraction times π, but sometimes an expression or a difference of two angles) and asks for degrees, or it gives degrees and asks for radians. The answer choices are numbers or multiples of π.
subtypes.method: 1) To go from radians to degrees, multiply by 180/π. To go from degrees to radians, multiply by π/180. 2) If the angle is a difference or an expression, convert the whole thing at once, because the conversion is linear.
subtypes.desmos: Type the radian expression times 180/π and Desmos gives you the degrees directly. This is quick if the fraction is awkward.
subtypes.trap: You multiply by the wrong factor (π/180 instead of 180/π), or you drop π from a radian answer and give a decimal that doesn't match any choice.

subtypes.name: Trig value of a radian angle via the unit circle
subtypes.tell: The question asks for sin, cos or tan of a radian angle that is large, negative or built from another angle (for example, one angle is k times another). The answer choices are exact values like ±1/2, ±√2/2, ±√3/2, ±√3 or ±1.
subtypes.method: 1) Work out the actual angle, then add or subtract multiples of 2π (or π, for tangent) until you get a coterminal angle between 0 and 2π. 2) Find the reference angle and the quadrant. 3) Use the special-triangle value, with the sign of x (for cos) or y (for sin) in that quadrant.
subtypes.desmos: Check that Desmos is in radian mode, then type cos(angle) and compare the decimal with the choices, for example 0.866 is √3/2. This is very reliable here.
subtypes.trap: You get the reference value right but the sign wrong for the quadrant. Other traps are working in degree mode, or reducing by 2π for tangent when reducing by π would also work, which leads to extra mistakes.

subtypes.name: Tangent lines, radii and inscribed triangles
subtypes.tell: The question says a line is tangent to the circle at a point, or two tangent segments come from one external point, or a triangle has one vertex at the center and two on the circle. It asks for a slope, another point on the tangent line, a side length, a perimeter or an area.
subtypes.method: 1) Draw the radius to the point of tangency. It is perpendicular to the tangent line, so the tangent's slope is the negative reciprocal of the radius's slope. 2) Two tangents from the same external point are equal in length and make right angles with the radii, so you get right triangles to use with the Pythagorean theorem or to find area. 3) Two radii make an isosceles triangle, so each of those sides equals r.
subtypes.desmos: Plot the center and the tangent point, then type the tangent line in point-slope form using the negative-reciprocal slope. Check which answer-choice point lies on it. This works well for the coordinate versions.
subtypes.trap: You use the radius's slope as the tangent's slope, or take the reciprocal without changing the sign. In triangles built from radii, a common mistake is forgetting that both radii equal r, or treating the distance from the center to the external point as a radius.
